items.summary: Evidence for large-scale differential rotation in the early universe and forward generation of its CMB topology by a primordial magnetic source — v1.8 reproducibility release Canonical 3° AC* is applied to the Planck PR3 SMICA, NILC, Commander, and SEVEM temperature reconstructions. AC* is a support-indexed multiscale spatial reconstructibility operator; direction, topology, and physical rotation arise only downstream. For canonical SMICA, 36,459 valid supports yield 27 large semiarcs. A separate high-resolution route uses 151 reciprocal HR1–HR2 structures to reconstruct an axis-free spherical tangent field. Blind recovery finds exactly four critical points of the represented lmax = 4 field: two spiral foci, one Node, and one Saddle. An all-sphere interval/Krawczyk analysis establishes completeness of this zero set. Focus A and Focus B are distinct oppositely rotating structures and admit a common transverse regular-vector realization in the coupled Einstein–Boltzmann state at recombination. Together with the differential-rotation reconstruction, polarization consistency, four-map comparison, perturbation tests, robustness controls, and exact propagation to z = 0, this provides evidence for large-scale differential rotation in the early universe. The independent forward-source test propagates a near-scale-invariant primordial magnetic source with nB = −2.9 to synthetic CMB skies and applies the same reconstruction without using the observed temperature map, critical-point geometry, Focus-A/Focus-B positions, measured H(J), or a magnetic-amplitude fit. One coordinate-blind realization generates the measured 2F+N+S topology and both rotational foci. The B-associated synthetic focus differs from the observed B focus only in the sign of a small divergent component; exact critical-point geometry is not reproduced. In eight matched phase-realization pairs, complete reconstruction occurs in five near-scale magnetic cases and none of the causal-white comparator cases, with three ties. The result establishes forward-generative capacity of the tested primordial magnetic source for the measured CMB topology and its two-focus rotational structure. It does not determine a unique magnetic spectrum, exclusivity among all possible source mechanisms, or an ensemble occurrence rate, and it is not a direct magnetic-helicity test. The release contains four public objects: Rambold_2026_CMB_v1p8.pdf — scientific manuscript. CMB_v1p8_interactive_scientific_viewer.zip — interactive scientific viewer. CMB_v1p8_python_pipeline.zip — executable analysis and replay code. CMB_v1p8_reproducibility_records.zip — scientific products, replay evidence, source-generation records, provenance, licences, manifests, SHA-256 bindings, and integrity records. Planck and WMAP FITS products are not redistributed and remain available from their public archives. Author-created scientific text and derived materials are released under CC BY 4.0 where applicable; original author-created software is released under the MIT License unless stated otherwise.
items.title: Evidence for large-scale differential rotation in the early universe from multiscale full-sky CMB reconstruction and forward generation of the reconstructed topology by a primordial magnetic source

items.summary: This v1.1 dataset provides the GenBank-synchronized genome annotation and reproducibility resources for Trichomonas tenax strain Hs-4:NIH (ATCC 30207). The current primary reference, annotation, CDS, and proteins follow NCBI Assembly GCA_061597355.1 and WGS JCCIQK000000000 (version JCCIQK010000000). The release includes the 212-contig structural backbone assembled from reads ≥15 kb, the final 178-contig public reference, complete annotation and evidence tables, contig-status and accession crosswalks, contamination-screening reports, Figure 1–6 source data, SOPs, and plotting and annotation scripts. Historical eggNOG, InterPro, homology, transcriptomic, and proteomic evidence, together with the original PRIDE search FASTA, are retained as versioned provenance and were not rerun on the standardized public GenBank protein sequences. Raw sequencing reads are available under BioProject PRJNA1457677, BioSample SAMN57469269, SRA Study SRP694902, and runs SRR38266486–SRR38266490. Proteomics data are available from PRIDE/ProteomeXchange under PXD084213 (https://doi.org/10.6019/PXD084213). Workflow code corresponding to this release is available in GitHub release v1.1.1 (https://github.com/yeh234/Ttenax-workflow/releases/tag/v1.1.1; commit 042bcc8db7eee584cb1c9b7653e0b313d3ccf8e0).
items.title: Trichomonas tenax Hs-4:NIH ATCC 30207 genome annotation and workflow release v1.1

Upstream geospatial preprocessing scripts are retained for methodological provenance and may require the original third-party source products and local GIS configuration. Original Landsat, GLC_FCS30D, WorldPop, and Copernicus DEM source archives are not redistributed in this record and should be obtained from their respective providers. items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/22983291 . General assessment This manuscript addresses an important and underappreciated problem in computational chemistry and molecular machine learning: apparent differences in predictive performance can arise from benchmark construction and target definition rather than from intrinsic superiority of one modelling approach over another. The distinction between literature-reported absorption maxima and calculated vertical excitation energies is scientifically important, and the emphasis on genuinely external validation is a clear strength of the work. However, I find the central conclusion stronger than the evidence presently described appears to support. The results convincingly show that model performance changes substantially across datasets and label conventions. They do not yet demonstrate that label definition, rather than model capability, is the principal cause of the apparent machine-learning advantage over TD-DFT. Several factors change simultaneously across the comparisons presented in the manuscript, including chemical domain, dataset provenance, transition assignment, computational protocol, sample size, and the nature of the machine-learning representation. These factors make it difficult to isolate label definition as the causal explanation. The manuscript raises a valuable methodological concern, but the title and several conclusions should either be moderated or supported by additional controlled analyses. Major comments 1. The title makes a stronger causal claim than the study design appears to establish The title states that benchmark label definition, "not model capability," explains the machine-learning advantage over TD-DFT. This is a strong exclusionary claim. The results show that the apparent ranking between a Gaussian-process model and quantum-chemical calculations changes between evaluation datasets. However, label definition is not the only property that changes between these datasets. Their chemical composition, source literature, distribution of chromophores, spectral range, experimental conditions, and possibly computational protocols also differ. Therefore, demonstrating that a GP performs differently on a dataset with transition-specific labels does not by itself establish that label definition is the cause of the difference. A substantially stronger test would use the same set of molecules with two alternative target definitions—for example, a literature-reported overall λmax and an independently assigned transition-specific λmax—and evaluate both methods against both labels. A paired analysis of this type would isolate label definition while holding molecular distribution constant. Unless such a controlled analysis is provided, I suggest moderating the central conclusion to state that label definition and dataset provenance are important contributors to the reported ML advantage rather than demonstrating that they fully explain it. 2. One Gaussian-process model cannot represent "machine-learning capability" generally The machine-learning side of the comparison is represented by a Gaussian process using 256-bit Morgan fingerprints. This is a relatively specific and comparatively simple model representation. The conclusions therefore apply directly to this GP/fingerprint model, but not necessarily to molecular machine learning more broadly. Modern λmax prediction methods may use larger fingerprints, graph neural networks, message-passing architectures, pretrained molecular representations, three-dimensional information, explicit solvent descriptors, or quantum-chemical features. Such models may respond differently to both chemical and label distribution shifts. items.summary: Predicted protein structures are now abundant but imperfect, and low per-residue confidence (pLDDT) is widely taken to mark regions worth refining. Before building a refiner, we test that premise directly: does low pLDDT actually predict AlphaFold contact error? Using a homology-controlled benchmark of matched AlphaFold-model (AFDB) inputs and experimental (PDB) targets, we compare AlphaFold and experimental contacts for every long-range residue pair and relate per-pair error to pLDDT. Across all 231 benchmark chains (4,208,603 long-range pairs; the effective sample is 231 chains, since pairs are pseudo-replicated within proteins), AlphaFold’s long-range contact calls are almost all correct — but this is expected, since most long-range pairs are non-contacts, so we focus on the contact-relevant errors. The per-pair contact-error rate is 0.0036 (95% bootstrap CI over chains 0.0033–0.0040), decomposed into false-positive contacts (asserted but absent) and missed real contacts. Low pLDDT is associated with elevated contact error (0.0089 below pLDDT 70 versus 0.0024 above, a 3.70× enrichment, 95% CI 3.3–4.1), but predicts it only weakly: the discrimination AUC of pLDDT as a contact-error score is 0.672 (95% CI 0.65–0.69), the best Youden threshold is near pLDDT 81 and the best F1 threshold near pLDDT 52, and pLDDT < 70 captures only 46% of all contact errors at sub-percent precision. False-positive (44%) and false-negative (56%) errors have different pLDDT profiles. Sequence/evolutionary information (ESM-2 contact probabilities) identifies these errors partially (AUC 0.61–0.63 for false positives, 0.66–0.86 for missed contacts), and low-confidence pairs that sit near a high-confidence anchor have a lower error rate (0.0074 versus 0.0090), suggesting anchor-based correction is a direction worth pursuing. Consistent with the weak localization of error, on a common subset of chains a hybrid Transformer–geometric refiner selected on validation precision cannot be distinguished from a copy-input baseline that trusts the AlphaFold structure (paired bootstrap over chains does not exclude zero difference). The practical conclusion is that on high-quality AlphaFold inputs there is little contact error to recover and pLDDT does not localize it well; useful refinement will need error-specific, evolutionarily grounded signal and may exploit high-confidence anchors. We release the benchmark, the characterization pipeline, and the code.
items.title: AlphaFold Contact Errors and pLDDT — Homology-Controlled Benchmark and Characterization

items.summary: This dataset provides the nationally consistent, footprint-level classification of residential building subtypes across the United States. It contains over 140 million building footprints classified into four distinct structural residential categories:  Single-Family Homes (SFHs), Townhouses (including duplexes), Apartments, and Mobile Homes .    The dataset is organized geographically and stored as individual, high-performance GeoPackage ( .gpkg ) files for each of the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia .   Data Schema (Attribute Fields) Each state-level GeoPackage contains the following standardized attribute columns:   geometry (Polygon) : The spatial boundary (polygon) of the building footprint. Res_type (Integer) : The classified residential structural subtype code: 1 = Single-Family Home (SFH) 2 = Townhouse (explicitly includes laterally attached row houses and semi-detached duplexes) 3 = Apartment 4 = Mobile Home height (Double) : The estimated physical height of the building in meters. Baseline heights are obtained from Microsoft Global ML footprints, with a minimum threshold of 4.2 m enforced (representing a typical one-story structure) and missing values imputed using local tract-level medians. type (String) : Building type tags from OSM building footprint (Limited coverage and varies by region).   Methodology and Classification Workflow The residential classifications were achieved using a novel, scalable hierarchical spatial workflow that integrates geometric building footprints with high-confidence administrative and demographic auxiliary data:   Multi-Source Footprint Integration: Geometry was compiled by merging Microsoft US Building Footprints, Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints, and OpenStreetMap (OSM) geometries. Non-residential structures were purged during preprocessing using OSM land-use layers and manual reclassification of OSM building tags. Mobile Home Identification: Candidate footprints located within spatial buffers around documented mobile home parks were classified using state-specific Random Forest (RF) models trained on footprint geometry (area, aspect ratio, rectangularity, and local density). High-confidence "seeds" were subsequently expanded using context-aware spatial promotion rules. Single-Family Home (SFH) Calibration: High-confidence SFHs were initially mapped using administrative address attributes. To prevent over- or under-counting, a size-ranked rule-based spatial promotion algorithm was implemented to sequentially classify candidate footprints until the counts aligned with rigorous state-level housing stock benchmarks derived from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. Townhouse and Apartment Discrimination: The remaining unclassified structures were categorized using a sequential, rule-based physical geometry and address-point pattern-recognition workflow. Duplexes and linear townhouses were distinguished from multi-family apartment blocks by evaluating physical constraints (convexity, height, and structural width) paired with the spatial density and linear alignment of internal address points from the National Address Database (NAD) . Spatial Context Completion: A final, iterative morphological distance-matching algorithm resolved any remaining unclassified structures based on local neighborhood class composition and physical architectural similarities (height, area, and aspect ratio).
items.title: Nationwide Footprint-Level Classification of Residential Building Subtypes for the United States

items.summary: Replication package for the paper "Use-dependent depreciation of intangible capital: thresholds, history dependence, and generative artificial intelligence." The paper studies a firm that accumulates an intangible stock — interpreted as the quality of its data estate — while the intensity with which it deploys a generative AI system accelerates the depreciation of that same stock. Optimal deployment therefore carries an intertemporal contamination wedge: the marginal value of scale is reduced by the shadow price of the stock times the marginal contribution of use to its decay. Under an S-shaped effectiveness function the problem admits three steady states, and optimal policy is history-dependent, separated by a threshold in the initial state obtained by value matching rather than by any local property of the unstable equilibrium. This package reproduces every number, table and figure reported in the paper. It contains three Python modules and no data: all results are generated from the model primitives and the stated parameter values. Contents model.py — model primitives and the numerical solver: steady states, stable manifolds, value functions, and the threshold by value matching. run_all.py — driver that reproduces all reported quantities and writes results/all_results.json . Runtime is approximately 25 minutes on a laptop; the Monte Carlo exercises dominate. make_figures.py — regenerates Figures 1 to 5 as PDF from the solver output. README.md — numerical methods, seeds, validation, and the classification scheme for perturbed draws. Requirements Python 3.10 or later with NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib. No other dependencies. Tested on NumPy 2.4, SciPy 1.17 and Matplotlib 3.10. Numerical methods Steady states are the roots of a scalar residual, bracketed on a grid and refined by Brent's method to a tolerance of 1e-13. Stable manifolds are obtained by eigen-decomposing the Jacobian at each saddle point, displacing along the stable eigenvector, and integrating the time-reversed canonical system with an adaptive Runge–Kutta scheme at relative tolerance 1e-11. Value functions exploit the identity between the costate and the derivative of the value function along the optimal path, with the constant of integration fixed by the perpetuity value at the steady state; this avoids forward integration, which is unstable off the saddle path. The threshold solves the value-matching condition on the overlap of the two manifold domains. Reproducibility All stochastic exercises use a fixed seed, numpy.random.default_rng(20260731) , so re-running reproduces the reported frequencies exactly. The shape of the effectiveness function is a parameter of the model rather than a code branch, so the exercises that compare specifications require no modification of the solver. Validation Value functions are cross-validated against direct time integration of discounted profit along the manifolds; the two computations agree to relative errors of 2.4e-6 and 6.2e-6 on the low and high branches. Single crossing of the difference of the two value functions is not established analytically, so the package records, for every perturbed draw admitting a threshold, whether that difference is strictly monotone on a 400-point grid. Draws on which the solver fails are reported as errors rather than discarded silently. Citation Please cite both this software and the associated paper. A CITATION.cff file is included.

Archaeological settlement observations are translated into 25 m cells nested within 250 m analytical zones, and model evaluation follows a pattern-oriented framework comparing observed and simulated change in occupied-zone density, settlement concentration, spatial extent, and nearest-neighbor spacing. The experimental design combines three organizational scenarios with stable, declining, and shock ecological conditions and independently varies landscape investment, producing 360 baseline simulations. Global sensitivity analysis additionally evaluates 16 parameters across 180 Latin hypercube sets. The repository provides the R workflow used for data preparation, simulation, validation, sensitivity analysis, figure generation, and manuscript tables, supporting transparent replication, methodological evaluation, comparative reuse in archaeological modeling, and facilitating critical assessment of alternative mechanisms underlying long-term settlement and socio-ecological change patterns.

items.summary: Artifact accompanying a manuscript under double-blind review . Author information is withheld until publication; a later version of this record will carry it, and the concept DOI is stable across versions. What this is. When two unlabelled subgroups of documents are compared by embedding similarity across languages, countries, corpora or periods, and the difference is read as evidence about those sources, no accuracy figure certifies that reading. within_language_baseline.py supplies the missing baseline: it measures the same subgroup contrast inside a single source, where no across-source relation can enter, and reports the residual with a bootstrap interval and an equivalence verdict against a margin declared in advance. The tool has no dependency on the accompanying study and runs on any corpus with three columns ( text , group , source ). It carries its own injection tests ( --selftest ). The bootstrap resamples documents rather than pairs and excludes duplicate draws of the same document from within-source pairs. Also included: the 36 frozen anchor correspondences used as the gold standard, the per-encoder CJK retrieval evaluation, the measured within-language and cross-country genre gaps, the equivalence intervals, an append-only correction record for the non-analytic genealogy fields of the frozen anchors, and anonymised review copies of the post hoc centring protocols and of the departure record. MANIFEST.sha256 covers every deposited file except itself.

items.summary: This release supports the study “Concurrent burned-area detections are associated with persistent agro-pastoral conversion after first forest loss in the Peruvian Amazon”. Version 1.1.0 adds Supplementary_Data_1_Active_Fire_Analysis.zip, containing the complementary historical NASA FIRMS MODIS and Suomi-NPP VIIRS analysis, the fixed protocol, input data, derived matching results, scripts, environment requirements, provenance, checksums, tests and independent verification results. Download and extract this ZIP without changing its folder structure, then open 08_VALIDACION_FUEGO_ACTIVO/START_HERE_REVIEWERS.md. The ZIP is 17,955,692 bytes and contains 59 files. The original cohort archive fire_loss_conversion_peruvian_amazon_v1.0.0.zip and its separate companion files are preserved unchanged. Those historical companions retain the original title, DOI, version and figure numbering. For this release, read START_HERE_VERSION_1_1_0.md and use CITATION_VERSION_1_1_0.cff. The original release remains available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21881539. The study uses a retrospective spatial cohort sampled on a systematic 0.01° lattice in stable forests of the Peruvian Amazon. Hansen Global Forest Change defines first loss during 2014–2021; MapBiomas Peru Collection 3 defines baseline and subsequent land cover; MapBiomas Fire and GABAM define concurrent burned-area detection categories. Persistent conversion requires anthropogenic cover in each of three consecutive post-loss years. The original archive reproduces analyses from derived panels, not the raster-to-panel extraction.
